podcast.title: Original Coca-Cola Jingle Recording (1971)
podcast.body: The New Seekers recorded the original radio jingle for the famous "Hilltop" Coca-Cola commercial with lyrics explicitly mentioning Coca-Cola, prior to its adaptation and release as a general pop single without product references. This initial recording established their sound as synonymous with the iconic ad. "The New Seekers recorded the original radio jingle with the lyrics about Coca-Cola."

podcast.title: US Touring Schedule (1971)
podcast.body: While touring America toward the end of 1971, the band managed to find time to enter a studio and record their own full-length version of "I'd Like to Teach the World to Sing," which was then released to compete directly on the charts with The Hillside Singers' version. "Meanwhile, the New Seekers, who were touring America toward the end of 1971, found time to get into a studio and record their own version."

podcast.title: Lawsuit Against Oasis
podcast.body: The New Seekers successfully sued Oasis due to the song "Shaker Maker" having a melody eerily similar to their worldwide hit, which originated from a Coca-Cola commercial jingle. The court case resulted in Oasis being ordered to make changes to their song. "And yes, there were similarities and yes, there was a lawsuit."

xref.title: Bonehead's Admission
xref.body: Guitarist Bonehead openly admitted that Oasis "ripped off" The New Seekers' melody for "Shaker Maker," acknowledging the legitimacy of the lawsuit. He quipped about changing brand loyalties after the incident. "We ripped it off. So they had the right to sue us. Fair enough, people will steal from other bands but change the lyrics. We did the same thing but kept some of the same lyrics. We drink Pepsi now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shaker Maker Lawsuit (Monty Python)
xref.body: In addition to The New Seekers, Oasis faced a second lawsuit over "Shaker Maker" from members of Monty Python's Flying Circus. They claimed the song sounded strikingly similar to a song from their 1973 TV sketch "How Sweet and Idiot." "Oasis was also sued by, wait for it, members of Monty Python's Flying Circus. They insisted that Shaker Maker sounded a lot like a song from a 1973 TV sketch called How Sweet and Idiot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shaker Maker Lawsuit (The New Seekers)
xref.body: Oasis was sued by The New Seekers due to the melody of "Shaker Maker" sounding too similar to a Coca-Cola commercial jingle that The New Seekers had turned into a worldwide hit. Oasis did not strongly contest the claim, with Liam Gallagher often humorously inserting parts of the Coke commercial song into live performances of "Shaker Maker." The court ordered Oasis to make changes to the song. "The upshot of this was a court case and Oasis was ordered to make changes to the song."
